title: Connectors
intro: Save a connection once, then select it in workflows, Custom Queries and reports. A connector stores the connection settings and encrypted credentials.
You need Manage connectors. Use your own database or service account. The pictures use a fictional read-only reporting account on an isolated Postgres database.

A fresh installation creates a target-warehouse connector for its configured database engine. These pictures use Target Warehouse (Postgres). Built-in queries and reports use the warehouse connector. Check their dependencies before changing it.
The host and port must be reachable from the OpenLDR server. In Docker, localhost means that container. Use your database service name and internal port when both services share a Docker network.
Creating a connector does not import records or run a workflow. Optional practice setup is at the end.

tasks.title: Choose the connection type
intro: Use the settings and account prepared for the service you want OpenLDR to reach. Choose the connection type before entering its fields.
steps: Select your account menu at the bottom of the main sidebar.
Select the page dots above the table.
Enter a name people can recognise when choosing a connector. The example uses Example reporting database. Keep passwords out of the name.
Set Category to Host for a built-in database, email or file connection.
Set Database type to the actual service. The example uses Postgres. This list also contains email and file services.

tasks.title: Enter the connection details and save
intro: Continue in the open connector sheet. The fields follow the service type you selected. This example uses Postgres.
steps: Fill Host, Port and Database. The example address is specific to this test installation. Use your server address.
Fill User and Password with the database account. A connection test does not establish which tables that account may read.
Match Use SSL to the database requirements. The local example leaves it off. Other service types have their own transport settings.
Select the dots in the connector sheet header.
tasks.result: The connector appears in the list and starts enabled. The Allowed plugin host column is a plugin network restriction. It is not the saved database address.

tasks.title: Test the saved connection
intro: Run a test after creating a connector or changing its credentials.
steps: Open the connector row dots and select Test.
Wait for Connection OK or a failure below the row menu. A successful connection does not prove a report query or email delivery succeeds.
tasks.result: The test uses the saved credentials from the OpenLDR server. Test outcomes appear in Audit.

tasks.title: Change settings or credentials
intro: Edit ordinary settings directly. Passwords stay blank after saving. Leave a password blank to keep it.
steps: On the correct connector row, open the dots and select Edit.
Verify the host, port, database and user. A set password shows a placeholder. Type a new password only when replacing it.
Open the sheet dots and select Save. The example leaves the password blank and keeps it. Test the connector again afterward.
tasks.result: The same connector remains available to its existing consumers. They use updated settings on their next run.

tasks.title: Find and temporarily disable a connection
intro: Disable a connector when you need to stop its use without deleting its stored settings.
steps: Use the search field to find a name, type or allowed plugin host.
Switch off Enabled on the correct row. Queries and workflows that need it can fail while it is disabled.
An off switch marks it disabled. Switch it on again when it may be used.
tasks.result: Disabling keeps the saved connector and credentials. It does not remove dependencies.

tasks.title: Remove a connection you no longer need
intro: Check dependent workflows, queries and reports before removal. Do not remove the warehouse connector just to clear the list.
steps: Open the row dots and select Remove.
Check the connector name. Choose Remove to delete it, or Cancel to keep it. The picture keeps this example for later tasks.
tasks.result: Confirming Remove deletes the connector and stored credentials. Anything that still refers to it fails until reconfigured.

tasks.title: Use Connectors on a phone
intro: The Host column is hidden at phone width. Open Edit to read a host connection address.
steps: Use search, then the row dots or Enabled switch.
Choose Edit from the row dots. The sheet fills the phone screen. Scroll inside it for longer service forms.

end.title: Choose the right type
paragraphs: SQL databases. Postgres, MySQL / MariaDB and Microsoft SQL have distinct connection settings. The selected connector controls the query dialect. For SQL Server instances and Windows domain accounts, use Diagnose connections.

Other host services. MongoDB, Redis, SMTP Email, IMAP Email, Gmail, Microsoft Outlook and SFTP show the fields relevant to their type. Use service credentials supplied by your operator. Gmail and Outlook types require an existing application registration and refresh token. SMTP uses the sending account and relay settings.

Plugin destinations. Choose Category Plugin, select an installed sink plugin, then enter Base URL, Username and Password together. When editing, leave all three blank to keep them, or replace all three. Install a sink through Marketplace if the selector is empty.
A node offers enabled connectors matching its required type. A missing connector can be disabled or have another type. Passwords do not belong in workflow labels or query text.

end.title: Use the command line
paragraphs: Follow Start here for CLI setup. From openldr_ce, use the commands below. Get the id from the list. CLI add, inspect, update, test and remove support host connectors. Plugin destinations use Studio.

An add file contains name, type and config. A patch file contains only fields to change. Omitted fields stay stored. Blank secrets keep existing values. Protect credential files and remove them after use.
html:
pnpm openldr connectors list
pnpm openldr connectors inspect <id>
pnpm openldr connectors add --file new-connector.json
pnpm openldr connectors update <id> --file connector-patch.json
pnpm openldr connectors test <id>
pnpm openldr connectors remove <id> --force

end.title: Optional practice setup
paragraphs: The tasks work with your own service account. For a disposable installation, ask the database operator to create a small test table and a read-only role. The screenshots use two fictional rows in guide_orders and guide_reader.

Do not copy the screenshot address or demonstration password into a real connector. Give a report account SELECT only on approved tables. Confirm both allowed and refused queries in your own database. This preview tested local Postgres connectivity. It did not test email delivery, cloud account authorization or file transfer.

end.title: Troubleshooting
paragraphs: Connection refused or timeout. Check the address from the OpenLDR server and the database firewall. Open row dots, then Diagnose for host connections.
Authentication failed. Check the account and database. Replace the password through Edit and test again.
SSL or certificate error. Ask the service operator which transport settings are required. SQL Server shows Encrypt and Trust server certificate.

A test passes but a query fails. Read the query error or workflow run. The account may lack access, the SQL may use another dialect, or the query may exceed its deadline. SQL connector queries have a 30-second limit.
Old query results remain visible. Check the error beside the connector selector. An earlier result table does not prove the latest run succeeded.

end.title: Related guides
paragraphs: Diagnose connections explains connection checks. Start here explains the CLI. Workflows and Custom Queries use saved connectors.
